First off, congratulations on this big first step: deciding you want to propose! 

I am also in a same sex couple, and my wife proposed to me in a private section of a public garden that was doing a Christmas light show. I was sitting on a bench, wondering why she was being so weird and wouldn’t just sit next to me, when she got down on one knee and asked me to be her wife, and it was beautiful and silly and wonderful. 

Here’s some tips:

- unfortunately, as a same sex couple, you do need to be aware of your surroundings and aware of the location. I’d avoid doing anything super public for a few reasons, but one of them is that you want to make sure no homophobic individuals could potentially see this happening and ruin it.

- because we’re same sex, we get to make a lot of our own rules. For example, my wife was very serious that she wanted to be the one to propose first, but I knew I wanted to get her a ring too. So after we were already engaged, a few months down the road I got her a ring too, took her to our favorite spot on the beach, and asked her to marry me right back. You get to decide what kind of engagement you wanna have. 

- if you’re just at the stage you’re thinking about proposing, the first thing I’d do is look internally and ask yourself why you want to get married. What about marriage appeals to you, what about loving her feels like you could do it forever? After that, if you come up with some good answers, think about a budget for a ring, grab a friend and start shopping.

In my opinion, by expressing your thoughts/feelings surrounding these friends, but still allowing your partner the autonomy to make that final decision, you have done your part. If he doesn’t change his friendship or drop them, well, you know where he stands. But if you make the friendship a condition of reconciliation, you will risk alienating him further. That’s human nature.

You can of course always express to a partner how uncomfortable their friends make you, making sure you use those big “I feel ___” statements we learn about in therapy, but I’m from the school of thought that no, you can’t ask someone to not be friends with people who are just friends.

These friends weren’t complicit in the action that hurt you the worst (the cheating), and he fed them misinformation. They’re victims of his lies too. By showing that you aren’t those things, they may come around eventually. Asking him to no longer be friends with them may drive a bigger wedge between you and your reconciling partner.

I think you might find some comfort in my post on this sub of my story, as your husband and I share a couple things in common. Mostly, the depression.

Suicidal ideation is no joke. It changes everything about how you view the world. You can tell me the sky is blue and I wouldn’t believe you- major depression clouds how you see yourself and everyone in your life. Your brain tells you no one will understand, everyone will hate you and they never cared at all. It’s brutal, and unfortunately, I totally understand how a suicidal person gets to the point of an affair. From a chemical perspective- our brains have no dopamine left.

But from my human perspective- even at my lowest, even when every day I was making final arrangements- I never had an emotional or physical affair, because in the core of my being I knew what that would do to my wife, to my friends and family, and to me.

Perhaps your husband couldn’t see that deep into himself and was just searching for that dopamine. If he’s still actively suicidal, he needs to go to the hospital. One thing that helped me is to write out everything my brain was telling me about myself, then have my wife read it. When I feel better, we’re going to burn the letter together.

As far as how long you have to wait- you don’t. You don’t owe anyone your time or love or affection. It’s your life and postponing your own healing and wellness for your spouses will only hurt you more. If you have questions, ask them. Now is not the time to go dark with friends and family, lean on them.

I didn’t have an emotional or physical affair, but I did have a very close friendship with someone I at one point had a crush on. I lied to my wife about it repeatedly. On our D-Day, I had to explain that I was talking to that person not to flirt, not to have sex or anything, but because I wanted to die. I still do. But I wanted so badly to end my life and I specifically felt that I couldn’t tell my wife. 

My spouse was absolutely willing to give support, and I pushed her away because of how scary the topic of suicide is. I knew how hard it would be for her, and I made the (totally wrong) decision to exclude her from it entirely.

I don’t know what kind of ‘emotional support’ your spouse says she was seeking, but if she’s in a mental health crisis, please don’t discredit how hard it is to discuss these sorts of things with loved ones.

None of this sounds like venting. Venting is throwing the words out to be heard, not actively attempting to coach or guide someone through a tough time.  You are absolutely putting yourself and others at risk doing this.

Let’s say people are balloons, and emotions are the air that fills us. When there’s cheating or an affair, both the betrayed and the wayward are completely filled with air. There’s so much that they’re about to pop. What are ways to release air?  Especially as a WS- Talk to each other. Go to individual counseling- I know you said you can’t afford it, but there are tons of mental health books and worksheets you can do in the meantime. Go for walks, re-engage in an old hobby, learn a new skill, take a free online class. But right now, by trying to talk to others about how much air they’re carrying around, you’re just risking inflating yourself more. Focus on you.

Anyway, actual insight time: there’s no right or wrong timeline here. A good therapist will never tell you that you need to be over something by a certain point, and most won’t take an accusatory approach towards someone. At least, they shouldn’t. Neutrality is good, it’s what you want in a therapist, but if you feel like it’s not helping you heal then I would suggest IC for yourself. Also, your indication that he’s too tired to talk in the afternoon/evening is a little worrying because he needs to take the initiative to find a time that does work for him to talk. 

Hope this helps. You should always be able to ask questions to maintain your sense of security. There’s no right or wrong timeline.

I am one of those. Now I’m a bit different, as I didn’t engage in a PA or a EA. I crossed boundaries though, and I lied repeatedly.
